standard_prerequisites.name: Transitive orientations characterize comparability graphs
standard_prerequisites.statement: An orientation is transitive when u->v and v->w imply that uw is an edge and is oriented u->w. Comparability graphs are exactly graphs admitting such an orientation.
standard_prerequisites.use: Each covering comparability graph carries its own transitive orientation; an edge belonging to both is allowed two orientations.

standard_prerequisites.name: Bipartite line graphs are perfect
standard_prerequisites.statement: Every induced subgraph of the line graph of a bipartite graph has chromatic number equal to clique number, by the classical bipartite edge-coloring theorem. Attaching pendant vertices preserves perfectness.
standard_prerequisites.use: Certify only perfectness of the explicit grid-with-leaves graph. No lower bound on the cover parameter is assumed.

standard_prerequisites.name: Elementary finite pigeonhole principle
standard_prerequisites.use: Convert four types of bad row vertices into three good vertices in one column after the nontrivial local orientation constraints are established.

core_obligations: Separate edge cover from partition, allowing overlap and independent orientations in two hypothetical covers.
Classify vertices that are not a middle point of a directed length-two path in either row orientation by four extremal types, and prove each type occurs at most once in a row.
Show that good vertices in one column must have the same row-orientation type and all column edges between them must lie exclusively in the other cover, since diagonal grid edges do not exist.
Force one vertex to be the middle of directed paths for both orientations and use its pendant edge to contradict transitivity in whichever cover contains that edge.
Construct the three-cover partition explicitly from row cliques, column cliques and pendant edges.

proof_roadmap.step: Identify grid rows, columns and pendant edges; perfectness is classical and these three edge classes give a comparability partition.
Assume two possibly overlapping transitive covers; at most four bad vertices per nine-vertex row, hence one four-vertex column contains three good vertices.
Nonexistent diagonal edges force all three row types to agree and the column triangle into the other orientation. Its middle vertex has no allowable pendant orientation in either cover.

difficulty_reason: The lower bound concerns covers with overlap, so ordinary edge-coloring arguments are insufficient. The proof couples two partial orders through row middle points and forbidden diagonal edges, then uses a pendant vertex to turn the resulting two-order middle-point obstruction into a contradiction. The finite counting step is simple; the nonroutine obligation is designing and checking this interacting orientation obstruction for all choices of cover and direction.

compared.difference: Existing claim is a recursive upper bound for partitions of integer-endpoint interval graphs after removing touching edges. This task is a finite perfect graph with exact cover and partition number3, using an orientation obstruction.

editorial_notes: H is the Cartesian product K9 square K4 with one new pendant vertex attached to each of its36 grid vertices; it has72 vertices. This is a finite graph, not an asymptotic construction.
The lower bound allows A and B to overlap. Their transitive orientations are considered separately, exactly as in source667; no partition assumption is inserted into the cover proof.

A row vertex isolated in one of the two oriented row subgraphs is both maximal and minimal. For the four-type counting argument it may be assigned either applicable status, with one fixed choice per orientation; same-type vertices still cannot share any covering edge.
The X_i/Y_i mentions in source661 and X_i in680 refer to the row and column families defined648-649; their names are dummy indices, and the author notation is retained.
This task uses the fixed source version2408.13523v2. The official abstract page lists a later v3; no unreviewed replacement of the selected source is made.

editorial_scope: One explicit finite graph and the exact values c(H)=p(H)=3, together with its perfectness. Interval graph asymptotic bounds, the earlier recursive upper bound, and the50-vertex personal-communication improvement are not counted.

review_checkpoints: A bad vertex may be isolated in A or B, so max/min labels need not be unique; choosing an applicable label per orientation is sufficient and uses only finite choices.
An A-good row vertex cannot have any A edge to a different row in its column, regardless of that edge direction, because one of its two row-path edges would require a forbidden diagonal.
If two column good vertices had different types, their connecting edge could be in neither A nor B. Three same-type vertices force a transitive triangle in the other cover.
At the middle of that triangle, a pendant edge in either cover forces a second edge incident to the pendant vertex, contrary to degree1.

issues_for_independent_review.detail: Check that an isolated row vertex being simultaneously max/min does not invalidate the four-type bound; the visible note fixes an arbitrary applicable type without changing the proof.
Judge the full dual-orientation obstruction after the explicitly allowed perfectness facts. Do not use the72-vertex size or paper status as difficulty evidence.
